newsitem.title: USA: NHL ICE HOCKEY - OLYMPIC EXPERIMENT HAS TEAM OFFICIALS WORRIED BUT ENTHUSED.
newsitem.headline: NHL ICE HOCKEY - OLYMPIC EXPERIMENT HAS TEAM OFFICIALS WORRIED BUT ENTHUSED.

text.p: Next year at this time officials of NHL teams will know whether sending the world's best hockey players to battle for gold and glory at the Nagano Olympics was a brilliant marketing move or a costly mistake.
In an unprecedented move, the National Hockey League will suspend operations for 17 days mid-season next year so players can represent their countries at the Winter Olympics.

What promises to be a dream tournament for fans, however, could prove a nightmare for general managers of NHL clubs who send their prime assets to the other side of the world when they should be home jockeying for playoff positions.

"It's a fait accompli, it's going to happen," said a fatalistic Jim Devellano, the Detroit Red Wings senior vice president of hockey operations whose club will supply several key members to the Russian team and others.

"My main concerns are player injury and player burnout," said Devellano, not quite opposing the league's decision to participate in the Games while expressing trepidation over adding the Olympics to the grueling NHL schedule.
"My concern is the Detroit Red Wings, quite frankly," he said. "It's a long season.

"We start training camp in September, if you get to the Finals it's June. This year we had the World Cup and next year there's the Olympics. And the best players also play in the NHL All-Star game," Devellano said. "It's a lot of hockey."
Injury is the greatest concern to NHL coaches and general managers, who will watch helplessly and hope their stars return from Japan in shape to resume the run for the Stanley Cup.
"We all understand (injuries) could happen," said Bob Clarke, general manager of the Philadelphia Flyers, who will serve in a similar capacity for Team Canada at Nagano.

"Major injury means you're going to miss one of your best players for the stretch drive," said Clarke, who lost superstar Eric Lindros for the first 23 games of the NHL season after he suffered a groin injury playing for Canada in the World Cup.

"I don't think any manager would be happy with the fact that seven or eight of his best players would be competing in the Olympics," admitted Clarke, who may be forced to watch as two of his own marquee players -- on opposing Olympic teams -- crash into each other with bone-crushing force.
Clarke was less concerned with physical exhaustion -- "they're athletes, they're well conditioned" -- than with the difficulty of the psychological switch in gears upon return.
"It's going to take a little time to get their emotional level back to NHL level. There's going to be a letdown, whether they're disappointed over losing or celebrating victory."
But Clarke, who led Philadelphia to two Stanley Cups as a player in the mid-1970s, wouldn't think of leaving one of his stars home for safe keeping.
"We will take the best Canadian team over that we possibly can," promised Clarke, whose second best player on the Flyers, John LeClair, will likely skate for the United States.

Also of concern is how the unusual mid-season disruption might affect those who don't make the trip to Nagano. A team that was building momentum in early February could well come out flat after a nearly three-week break.

But Pierre Lacroix, general manager of the Stanley Cup champion Colorado Avalanche, thinks the layoff could prove beneficial, if players "use the break in the right fashion to heal small injuries or to regroup with families."
And while as worried about losing key players as his peers, Lacroix is an unabashed fan of the Olympic plan.
"It's a great thing for the great game of hockey," he gushed.

"It's a great opportunity for the rest of world to see this game. Finally they are going to see the best players," added Lacroix, who expects his club to contribute players to the German and Russian squads as well as sending stars Joe Sakic to Team Canada and Peter Forsberg to the Swedish team.

"A tournament that creates high emotion like the Olympics is always a plus in a player's life. All the players will come out of the Olympic experience feeling like they've gained something," Lacroix predicted.
"It's going to be an unbelievable tournament."
Clarke also suspects that any conflict he may feel between the quests for the Stanley Cup and Olympic gold will fade as next February rolls around.
"When the plane leaves and you're sitting there with your team going to Japan, I think the thrill for players and coaches and management will be unbelievable."
